item.title: Bank of Canada preview: 81% chance of first hike in a year to 2.50%, economists split
item.description:
With a hike close to fully priced, the Canadian dollar’s reaction will likely turn on the Monetary Policy Report and forward guidance rather than the decision itself. A hold would be a sizeable surprise, likely sending the loonie sharply lower and pulling short-dated Canadian yields down. A hike signalling further tightening would support the currency and push the front end higher, while a “one and watch” message could see pricing for a follow-up move by March trimmed. Oil is the external wildcard: higher crude both lifts Canadian headline inflation and supports the commodity-linked loonie, so further energy price gains would reinforce the hawkish case. Friday’s August GDP data could then quickly test whatever guidance the bank delivers.

---

Busy week ahead (and I haven't even mentioned the elephant in the room yet!)

  • BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike
  • Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation

---

A week ago the Bank of Canada looked set to sit tight, but one hint from Governor Macklem about higher inflation forecasts has put a first hike in a year firmly on the table.

Summary:

  • The Bank of Canada announces its decision on Wednesday, with markets pricing an 81% chance of a 25bp hike to 2.50%, which would be its first move in a year
  • A Reuters poll found 19 of 34 economists expect a hike, and a majority see one more by March 2027; the previous poll had 80% expecting a hold through 2026
  • Governor Tiff Macklem said the bank’s inflation forecasts are likely to be revised higher, remarks markets read as a signal of tightening
  • HSBC says survey data, notably rising long-term consumer inflation expectations, point to a hike despite soft hard data
  • TD does not share the market’s conviction, citing limited inflation breadth and near-term uncertainty
  • The decision and Monetary Policy Report are due at 09:45 ET (13:45 GMT); August GDP follows on Friday

The Bank of Canada is expected to raise interest rates for the first time in a year on Wednesday, with markets pricing an 81% chance of a 25 basis point increase that would take its key policy rate to 2.50%, although some economists remain unconvinced the move is warranted.

Expectations have shifted rapidly. A Reuters poll conducted from October 21 to 23 found that 19 of 34 economists now forecast a hike this week, and a majority also expect one more increase by the end of March 2027, taking the rate to 2.75%. That marks a sharp reversal from the previous poll, when 80% of respondents expected the bank to hold at 2.25% through the end of 2026.

The catalyst was Governor Tiff Macklem, who told reporters that the bank’s quarterly inflation projections, to be published alongside Wednesday’s decision, are likely to be revised higher. Markets took the comments as a hint that tightening is coming, and futures pricing for an October hike jumped from around 30% before the remarks to roughly three in four, according to Reuters. Many economists switched their calls from a hold to a hike over the following week.

HSBC analysts said recent survey data suggest a hike is likely, pointing in particular to a rise in long-term consumer inflation expectations, even though other hard economic data have been on the soft side.

Not everyone agrees. TD analysts said they do not share the market’s conviction that rates will rise, citing limited breadth in inflation and uncertainty over the near-term outlook. Others have argued that energy-driven price increases are unlikely to feed through to underlying inflation on their own, while still expecting the bank to tighten if price pressures broaden. Weakness in the labour market earlier in the autumn had also led markets to push back expectations for a move toward December.

The decision and the accompanying Monetary Policy Report are due at 09:45 ET (13:45 GMT) on Wednesday. With a hike largely priced, the bank’s updated forecasts and guidance on further tightening are likely to drive the market reaction. August GDP data, due on Friday, will offer an early test of the outlook. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Standard Chartered sees debt-funded share of AI capex rising to 40% in 2027 from 25%
item.description:
A growing reliance on debt to fund AI infrastructure ties the tech trade more closely to the rates outlook, so hawkish central bank signals, including a Fed on a hiking path, could weigh harder on capex-heavy names than in earlier phases of the boom. Credit markets are likely to see heavier tech bond issuance, and investors may demand wider spreads if deployment delays push back revenue. Next week’s Big Tech results are the near-term catalyst: firm capex guidance paired with clearer monetisation would ease funding concerns, while rising spend without visible returns could deepen the mixed share-price reactions already evident. The bank’s preference for diversification points to potential rotation toward sectors and regions outside concentrated US tech leadership.

---

---

The AI build-out is increasingly running on borrowed money, and Standard Chartered wants proof of returns from Big Tech before adding to riskier corners of the sector.

Summary:

  • Standard Chartered says Q3 US tech earnings point to strong compute demand and continued growth in capital spending
  • The bank keeps a positive long-term view on AI investment but flags short-term funding and execution risks, and prefers not to add exposure to higher-risk tech for now
  • It expects debt-financed AI capex to rise from about 25% of the total in 2026 to around 40% in 2027, increasing sensitivity to interest rates
  • Deployment delays could defer revenue while financing costs continue, though wider commercial adoption of AI could generate cash flow and reduce reliance on borrowing
  • Next week’s Big Tech earnings will be assessed for capex guidance, funding and monetisation trends, with market leadership concentrated and share-price reactions mixed
  • The bank remains invested but defensively positioned, favouring diversification across sectors and regions

Third-quarter earnings from US technology companies point to robust demand for computing power and ongoing expansion in capital expenditure, but the growing role of debt in funding the artificial intelligence build-out is adding new risks, according to Standard Chartered.

In its weekly market review, the bank said it retains a favourable long-term view on AI investment, while warning about funding and execution risks in the near term. For now, it prefers not to increase exposure to the higher-risk parts of the technology sector. Recent results suggest that major tech companies remain committed to expanding their AI infrastructure, the bank said.

The central concern is how that expansion is being paid for. Standard Chartered expects borrowing to take on a larger share of the burden as companies spend more on data centres and computing equipment. It forecasts that debt-financed AI capex will rise from about a quarter of total AI capex in 2026 to around 40% in 2027. Greater dependence on debt makes the sector more sensitive to interest rates, the bank said, while any delays in deploying new capacity could push back revenue recognition even as financing costs continue to build.

There is a potential offset. The bank expects broader commercial adoption of AI services to generate additional cash flow, which could help companies fund further infrastructure investment with less need for external borrowing.

That makes next week’s Big Tech earnings a key test. Standard Chartered said it will look to the results for greater clarity on capex guidance, funding plans and progress in monetising AI. It noted that the reporting season carries added uncertainty, with market leadership still concentrated in a small group of stocks and share-price reactions becoming more mixed.

Looking further ahead, the bank expects equity performance to depend more on companies delivering stronger earnings than on further expansion in valuations. It highlighted sustainable AI financing, commercial returns on infrastructure spending and broader profit growth beyond technology as the factors investors should watch. Standard Chartered said it remains invested but defensively positioned, favouring diversification across sectors and regions. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike
item.description:
A hold is largely the base case, so the yen and JGB yields are likely to take their cue from the language rather than the decision. A formal declaration that underlying inflation has reached 2%, a Takata dissent and any shift by Ueda toward “next meeting” phrasing would together read as hawkish, supporting the yen and pushing short-end yields higher as markets price a December move. Higher crude prices are a key upside risk, with oil already reigniting upstream cost pressure and feeding the BOJ’s concern about inflation overshooting. A guarded Ueda who stresses a broad review of financial conditions could see December pricing trimmed and the yen soften.

---

Also this week:

  • Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation

--- The BOJ is expected to stand pat on rates while quietly moving the goalposts, from getting inflation up to 2% to stopping it from running beyond it, which keeps December firmly in play.

Summary:

  • Daiwa expects the BOJ to keep rates unchanged at its October meeting, with October surveys showing softer household and business inflation expectations
  • The board is likely to conclude that underlying inflation has reached 2%, shifting policy from lifting inflation toward stabilising it around that level
  • Board member Hajime Takata may again propose a rate hike, while Naoki Tamura is seen backing a hold after September’s increase
  • Daiwa expects the Outlook Report to raise the FY26 growth forecast to 0.8% from 0.6% and FY27 core CPI to 2.5% from 2.4%, and to trim FY26 core-core CPI to 2.4%
  • Higher crude prices have reignited upstream inflation pressure, and the BOJ’s policy rate already sits above the lower end of its estimated neutral range of around 1% to 2.5%
  • Ueda’s press conference will be watched for December hints, particularly any shift from “every meeting” language toward the next meeting

The Bank of Japan is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, but the decision could still mark an important shift in its policy thinking, according to a preview from Daiwa Securities. The broker expects the board to conclude that underlying inflation has reached 2%, a step that would move the central bank from a phase of lifting inflation toward its target to one focused on keeping it stable around that level.

Daiwa cited media reports that economic conditions and prices have continued to track the BOJ’s outlook since September, and that policymakers do not see upside inflation risks as strong enough to justify back-to-back rate increases. Surveys published in October also showed inflation expectations among households and businesses easing. Even so, concern about an inflation overshoot remains high. Cost pass-through is broadening at the consumer level, and rising crude oil prices have revived upstream price pressures, with some within the BOJ expecting pass-through to accelerate into next year.

Governor Kazuo Ueda signalled the change in tone earlier this month, saying that with underlying inflation now close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and is aiming to stabilise it. Daiwa expects the Outlook Report to replace its description of inflation as approaching 2% with wording that it is broadly consistent with the target, and argues that if the report continues to flag upside inflation risks, that would provide grounds for considering an early hike.

The broker expects board member Hajime Takata to dissent and propose a hike, as he did in July, citing strong global demand, including for AI-related products. Naoki Tamura, who has spoken of raising rates every few months toward a neutral level of around 2%, is seen supporting a hold so soon after September’s increase.

On forecasts, Daiwa expects the board to lift its FY26 growth projection to 0.8% from 0.6% and FY27 core inflation to 2.5% from 2.4% on the back of higher oil prices, while trimming FY26 core-core inflation slightly to 2.4%. The report is unlikely to factor in a planned cut to the consumption tax on food, which Daiwa estimates could lower core inflation by roughly 1.5 percentage points in FY27.

Ueda’s post-meeting press conference will be pivotal. Daiwa will watch whether he keeps describing rate decisions as being made at each meeting or shifts toward language pointing to the next meeting, which markets could read as a stronger signal of a December hike. With the policy rate already above the lower end of the BOJ’s estimated neutral range, his assessment of financial conditions will also shape expectations for how quickly further tightening follows.

---

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Strategy bitcoin purchases shrink as buybacks take priority ahead of earnings
item.description:
Saylor skips his Sunday bitcoin chart as Strategy heads into earningsStrategy chairman Michael Saylor did not share his usual Sunday bitcoin chart this week. Bitcoin watchers read that as a sign that Strategy (MSTR), the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, may have paused its buying. Saylor was active on X on Sunday: he described bitcoin as “the moat” in a reply to Jack Dorsey. But the chart that usually comes before a purchase announcement did not appear. A missing chart is a signal, not a confirmation. The company’s Monday filing will settle the question, and its third-quarter results follow on Thursday.

---

Earlier:

  • Bitcoin buyers are fighting back, but sellers aren't finished. Here are the two prices swing traders should watch

---

What is the ‘orange dot chart’?For more than a year, Saylor has posted a snapshot of Strategy’s bitcoin tracker to X almost every Sunday. The chart plots the value of the company’s holdings over time, and each orange dot marks a purchase. The graphic has historically come before a Monday 8-K filing confirming that Strategy bought bitcoin the previous week. The caption changes each week, but the message is usually the same: more coins are coming. Over the past two weeks, Saylor captioned the chart with variations on finding room for more orange, and both posts were followed by purchase disclosures. The pattern is not a fixed rule. In July, after a large bitcoin sale, Saylor posted the tracker with an unusually vague caption saying the orange dots tell only part of the story, and the post a week earlier had come before the largest sale in company history. A missing chart suggests a pause, but it does not prove one. The buying has already slowedThe size of recent purchases is the bigger story. Strategy bought 267 BTC for about $22.1 million at an average of $82,900 per coin in the week to October 18. That followed a 250 BTC purchase for about $21.5 million the week before. Earlier in the year, single weekly purchases topped 20,000 BTC. The latest purchase was funded almost entirely by selling 140,872 MSTR shares through the company’s at-the-market program. Over the same week, the company spent far more on its own securities. It used $193.1 million to buy back 1.94 million shares of its STRC preferred stock, and the board raised its digital credit securities repurchase program from $2 billion to $3 billion. STRC is one of Strategy’s preferred shares, which pay holders a regular dividend. Buying them back below their $100 face value reduces the company’s future dividend costs. Michael Saylor 'Found More Room for Orange' as Strategy Adds 267 Bitcoin - Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) - BenzingaStrategy has also sold bitcoin this year. It reported selling 32 BTC in early June, its first disclosed sale since a 2022 tax-loss transaction. It then sold 3,588 BTC for about $216 million to fund preferred stock distributions and top up its US dollar reserve. A further 1,638 BTC was sold between July 27 and August 2 at an average of $63,957, with the proceeds split between preferred dividends and STRC buybacks. Even so, Strategy’s holdings stand at 848,517 BTC, bought for about $64 billion at an average of $75,446 per coin, more than 4% of bitcoin’s total supply. What could change the readA pause would not be new. In September, Saylor’s chart returned after a two-week buying break, and purchases resumed. The company also has the money to buy. As of October 4, its USD Reserve stood at $4.88 billion, with $833.4 million in USD Cash. A larger purchase disclosed on Monday would undercut the slowdown story. Another quiet week on bitcoin, alongside continued buybacks, would reinforce it. bitcoinWhat to watch nextThe first test is Monday’s 8-K filing, which will show whether Strategy bought, sold or held bitcoin last week, and how much it spent on buybacks.Next come third-quarter results. Strategy reports after the US close on Thursday, October 29, and will host a live webinar at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time. The headline profit should hold few surprises, since the fair value of the company’s bitcoin was already above its cost basis as of September 30. Management’s comments on funding, dividends and the balance between buybacks and bitcoin purchases are likely to matter more. For bitcoin traders, the practical point is that Strategy has been a steady buyer through much of this cycle. If its weekly purchases stay small, the market loses a reliable source of demand. Watch the size of the purchases, not just whether there are any.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation
item.description:
With a hike close to fully priced, the New Zealand dollar’s reaction is likely to hinge on guidance rather than the move itself, and the risk is asymmetric: a hold would catch markets badly offside and could trigger a sharp kiwi selloff. A hike paired with a clear tightening bias would be the most supportive outcome for the NZD and would push front-end yields higher, while “wait and see” language could see some of the priced peak trimmed. Oil remains the key external driver: further gains in crude linked to the Middle East conflict would feed straight into New Zealand’s fuel-heavy inflation outlook and strengthen the case for more hikes into 2027. AUD/NZD traders also face back-to-back central bank risk, with the RBA expected to hike again on November 3.

---

A pause looked likely in September, but rising fuel costs and a sliding kiwi have turned Wednesday’s RBNZ meeting into a near-certain pre-election hike.

Summary:

  • Economists and markets expect the RBNZ to raise the OCR by 25bp to 3% on Wednesday, its third straight hike after moves in July and September
  • Expectations for a pause after September have reversed as oil prices surged, the New Zealand dollar weakened and inflation pressures proved sticky
  • Annual CPI eased to 3.7% in the September quarter, below the RBNZ’s 3.9% forecast, but some economists see the December quarter above 4.5%
  • Markets price roughly a 90% chance of a hike and a peak near 3.5% by February; Westpac sees the OCR possibly reaching 4% by September 2027
  • ASB warns that a hold would likely sink the kiwi, with guidance on further tightening seen as the key market driver
  • The decision is due at 01:00 GMT Wednesday (21:00 ET Tuesday), ahead of New Zealand’s November 7 general election

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is widely expected to raise its Official Cash Rate by 25 basis points to 3% on Wednesday, delivering a third consecutive hike as rising fuel costs and a weak currency threaten to push inflation further above its target band.

The call marks a turnaround from just weeks ago. After the RBNZ lifted the OCR to 2.75% in early September, Governor Anna Breman hinted at a pause, and bank economists were divided on whether October would bring another move. That debate has largely closed. According to interest.co.nz, economists at the country’s major banks now see a hike as almost certain, pointing to the surge in oil prices, further weakness in the New Zealand dollar and persistently sticky price pressures.

A Bloomberg survey also found that a majority of economists expect the OCR to rise to 3% this week. Inflation slowed in the third quarter, with annual CPI easing to 3.7% from 4.1% in June and coming in below the RBNZ’s 3.9% forecast. Many analysts expect it to accelerate again in the fourth quarter, however, with some projecting a December quarter reading of around 4.7%, which would leave inflation outside the 1% to 3% target band for longer than the central bank had projected.

Markets are positioned accordingly. ASB economists said pricing implies roughly a 90% probability of a 25 basis point increase, with a peak cash rate of around 3.5% expected by February. Westpac sees the tightening cycle running further, with the OCR possibly reaching 4% by September 2027. ASB has also warned that the prospect of hikes has been supporting the New Zealand dollar, and that a decision to hold would likely send the currency lower.

The timing adds a political dimension. The meeting falls just 10 days before the November 7 general election, although economists broadly expect the committee to set policy on economic grounds alone. Some argue the bank should go beyond a single move and signal that more tightening is coming, while others expect a short statement that leaves options open.

The decision is due at 01:00 GMT on Wednesday (21:00 ET on Tuesday). With a hike largely priced, the tone of the accompanying statement is likely to determine the market reaction. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin buyers are fighting back, but sellers aren't finished. Here are the two prices swing traders should watch
item.description:
Bitcoin is approaching an important decision point for swing traders. Sellers have demonstrated their strength, but buyers are showing signs of defending the $80,000 area. The latest investingLive tradeCompass maps two conditional scenarios: bullish above $80,860 and bearish below $79,870.

The challenge is distinguishing a temporary rebound from a more durable recovery, or a brief dip from another significant breakdown.

Bitcoin tradeCompass: The bullish and bearish levels

The tradeCompass identifies two directional thresholds. Traders can use them to prepare for either outcome rather than commit to a prediction.

Bullish Bitcoin above $80,860

A sustained move above $80,860 would strengthen the case that Bitcoin's recent stabilization is developing into a more meaningful recovery.

The potential bullish profit targets are:

The first target at $81,770 represents the initial opportunity to secure a partial profit. The higher targets provide objectives if buying momentum develops into a more substantial swing.

Importantly, the bullish threshold has already been tested. On October 25, Binance BTC/USDC traded as high as approximately $80,942 before retreating below $80,860. A subsequent market snapshot around 20:04 UTC showed Bitcoin near $80,453.

That brief crossing is not sufficient by itself to establish a confirmed breakout or an executed trade. Traders considering the bullish scenario should reassess whether price can regain and hold above the threshold.

Bearish Bitcoin below $79,870

A sustained breakdown below $79,870 would suggest that the latest attempts to establish support have failed, potentially putting sellers back in control.

The bearish profit targets are:

The first two targets are relatively close to the bearish threshold. The third and fourth require more meaningful downside continuation.

A breakdown would become more convincing if Bitcoin struggled to recover above the breached level after initially falling through it.

Between $79,870 and $80,860, the tradeCompass remains neutral. This is a decision zone, not a requirement to trade. Neither a failed bullish attempt nor a minor decline inside the zone automatically activates the bearish scenario.

Bitcoin sellers have the bigger trend, but buyers are challenging them

The recent price action presents an interesting conflict between different trading timeframes.

On October 22, Bitcoin experienced renewed selling pressure that undermined an earlier recovery attempt. The accompanying CME Bitcoin futures analysis showed elevated trading participation and a close near the lower end of the session's range.

That matters because sellers were not merely pushing prices temporarily lower. They demonstrated an ability to sustain downward pressure during an important session.

However, the subsequent price action offers a reason not to become overly committed to the bearish outlook.

On October 24, Bitcoin briefly traded down toward $79,133 on Binance BTC/USDC before recovering. That rejection was accompanied by unusually high trading activity in the relevant hourly observation.

Additional shorter-term observations on October 25 showed repeated unsuccessful attempts to sustain lower prices and improving intraday lows around the $80,000 to $80,440 region.

These developments suggest that buyers are becoming more willing to defend the lower trading area.

There is an important distinction, however, between buyers defending support and buyers establishing a new bullish trend.

The daily structure still showed bearish characteristics in the October 25 analysis. The shorter-term recovery signals had not overturned that broader weakness.

For Bitcoin swing traders, this distinction matters. A convincing move above $80,860 could create an attractive tactical bullish opportunity without necessarily confirming that the broader correction has ended.

Likewise, another successful defense around $80,000 does not guarantee that support will hold on the next test.

The first profit target matters for more than taking profits

One of the most useful principles of the investingLive tradeCompass is that trade management deserves as much attention as the initial direction.

For either scenario, traders following the suggested plan can consider two actions after reaching TP1:

  1. Take a partial profit on the position.

  2. Move the protective stop on the remaining position to the actual entry price.

For a bullish trade, that consideration arises at $81,770. For a bearish trade, it arises at $79,630.

The purpose is to reduce the remaining exposure while allowing part of the position to participate if a larger move develops.

Moving a stop to entry does not guarantee a completely risk-free outcome. Trading costs, spread, slippage and execution conditions can still produce losses.

Traders should also establish an appropriate initial protective stop before entering a position. The tradeCompass's opposite activation threshold is not automatically the appropriate stop, and position size should reflect the risk of the actual setup.

Why swing traders should avoid repeatedly chasing the same signal

The tradeCompass has another principle intended to discourage overtrading.

Each published tradeCompass allows a maximum of one completed bullish trade and one completed bearish trade under its suggested discipline.

If a trader enters a long position and that trade eventually concludes, the bullish opportunity from this particular publication is considered used, regardless of whether the trade made money, lost money or reached only its first profit target.

The same rule applies independently to the bearish scenario.

An unfilled order does not count as a completed opportunity, and an open position with a remaining runner is still part of the original trade.

The opposite direction can remain available if its conditions subsequently develop, but reversing after a losing trade should not be automatic.

This approach encourages selectivity rather than repeatedly entering whenever Bitcoin fluctuates around a familiar price.

What could make Bitcoin's next swing more convincing?

The bullish and bearish scenarios have different confirmation requirements, but they share an important principle: crossing a level is not the same as sustaining a move beyond it.

For bulls, the next improvement would be a renewed move above $80,860 that can hold. Depending on the trader's existing strategy, confirmation might involve a candle closing above the threshold, a successful retest or another independently validated entry signal.

For bears, renewed acceptance below $79,870 would indicate that the recovery attempts around $80,000 are failing.

The extended targets in both directions should be understood as potential objectives rather than forecasts of imminent moves.

For now, the central Bitcoin question is whether buyers can turn their recent defensive activity into sustained upside progress.

Above $80,860, the bullish tradeCompass becomes relevant. Below $79,870, the bearish opportunity becomes relevant. Between those levels, patience may be the more useful position.

For a fuller explanation of how these conditional scenarios work, read the investingLive guide to using tradeCompass.

The Fed may leave interest rates unchanged this week. So why could Bitcoin still move?

Bitcoin traders have another important event to watch this week: the US Federal Reserve's interest rate decision on Wednesday, October 28.

The Federal Reserve, often called the Fed, influences how expensive it is to borrow money. Higher interest rates can make safer investments, such as government bonds, more attractive compared with riskier assets like Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.

But markets often react more to what the Fed says about future interest rates than to the actual decision.

What does the market expect?

According to an October 20 Reuters survey cited in the analysis, 94 out of 100 economists expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% this Wednesday.

The supplied survey also reports that all 100 economists anticipate another rate increase in December.

That means leaving rates unchanged in October would not be particularly surprising. What could move Bitcoin is whether the Fed sounds more or less concerned about inflation and the need for further rate increases.

Three possible scenarios for Bitcoin and crypto

Scenario 1: Expected outcome - The Fed holds rates and remains cautious

The Fed leaves interest rates unchanged and signals that another increase in December is still likely.

Because markets already expect this, the decision might not provide Bitcoin with a strong reason to rise or fall.

Possible crypto reaction: Bitcoin remains choppy and directionless, with buyers and sellers continuing to compete around $80,000. Altcoins may also struggle to establish a convincing recovery.

For our tradeCompass, Bitcoin remaining between $79,870 and $80,860 would favor patience rather than forcing a directional trade.

Scenario 2: Bullish surprise - The Fed signals fewer rate increases

The Fed leaves rates unchanged but unexpectedly suggests that inflation is becoming less concerning, making another rate increase in December less certain.

This would be meaningful because investors expecting higher interest rates might suddenly reconsider their outlook.

Possible crypto reaction: Bitcoin rallies as investors become more willing to take risks. Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies could also benefit, particularly if the US dollar and bond yields decline.

For our tradeCompass, a sustained break above $80,860 would bring the bullish targets into focus, starting at $81,770, followed by $85,200.

Scenario 3: Bearish surprise - The Fed raises rates or warns of more hikes

The Fed unexpectedly increases interest rates immediately, or leaves them unchanged but suggests that inflation is serious enough to require several additional increases.

This would be a more aggressive message than markets currently expect.

Possible crypto reaction: Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies could sell off sharply as investors reduce exposure to riskier assets. A stronger US dollar and rising bond yields could add pressure.

For our tradeCompass, a sustained move below $79,870 would activate the bearish scenario, with initial targets at $79,630 and $79,310. If selling continues, the lower targets become relevant.

What should Bitcoin traders watch?

The Fed decision is scheduled for 2:00 p.m. New York time on Wednesday, followed by the press conference at 2:30 p.m.

Traders can also watch the US dollar and Treasury yields for clues about how financial markets interpret the announcement.

And there is another potential catalyst on Thursday, October 29, when important US inflation (PCE) and economic growth (GDP) figures are scheduled for release.

The important lesson: Markets respond to surprises, not simply whether news sounds good or bad. Even a decision to do nothing can move Bitcoin if the Fed's message changes what investors expect next.

That is another reason to use the tradeCompass as a conditional trading map, rather than trying to predict the Fed's decision or Bitcoin's immediate reaction.

Educational only. Trade at your own risk. Cryptocurrency markets can be highly volatile, and losses may exceed expectations when trading with leverage.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend - China warns of countermeasures as US Treasury widens tech investment curbs to biotech
item.description:
The proposal adds to already tense US-China relations and keeps headline risk elevated for Chinese technology and biotech stocks, including US-listed ADRs and the Hang Seng Tech index. Biotech is the sector most directly exposed, since it is the newly targeted industry and has relied more heavily on cross-border funding than areas already under restriction. Beijing has not named the countermeasures it might take, and that vagueness tends to keep investors cautious until the response becomes clear. A long public comment period leaves time for negotiation, but it also stretches the uncertainty out for months, which could weigh on risk appetite toward China-exposed assets and the offshore yuan if rhetoric escalates.

--

Washington wants to stop US capital from funding China’s next generation of strategic technology, and Beijing is signalling that it will not take the move quietly.

Summary:

  • On Thursday the US Treasury proposed a rule expanding the Outbound Investment Security Program, tightening limits on US investment in hypersonics, quantum, high-performance computing, supercomputing and AI in China, Russia and North Korea
  • The rule also adds biotechnology to the targeted sectors, an addition sought by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
  • China’s commerce ministry said on Saturday the move discriminatorily widens China-related restrictions, overstretches national security and would damage bilateral economic ties
  • Beijing said it will monitor developments and reserves the right to take unspecified countermeasures
  • The proposal faces a public comment period before a final rule is issued
  • Separately, the State Department this week sanctioned five Chinese companies linked to former Google engineer Linwei Ding, convicted this year of stealing AI trade secrets, drawing further objections from Beijing

China has urged the United States to reconsider a proposed rule that would further restrict American investment in its technology sector, warning that the measure would harm trade relations and that Beijing reserves the right to retaliate.

China’s commerce ministry voiced firm opposition on Saturday in a statement carried by the state-run Global Times, according to a report by The Hill. A ministry spokesperson said the proposal widens China-related investment restrictions in a discriminatory way and described it as a classic example of stretching the concept of national security too far. The ministry said it would watch subsequent developments closely, warned the rule would damage economic ties between the two countries, and said China retains the right to take corresponding measures, without specifying what those might be.

The US Treasury Department unveiled the proposal on Thursday. It would expand existing restrictions under the Outbound Investment Security Program covering hypersonic systems, quantum information technologies, high-performance computing, supercomputing and artificial intelligence. The program aims to stop a small group of countries designated as foreign adversaries, namely China, Russia and North Korea, from using US capital to advance their own technological capabilities.

The proposed rule would also bring the biotechnology industry within the program’s scope, an addition that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had pushed for, according to a department press release. Bessent said the changes would strengthen the program and prevent adversaries from using American investment to build critical technologies that threaten US national security.

The measure must go through a public comment period before Treasury issues a final version, leaving room for revisions and for further diplomatic exchanges in the meantime.

The proposal lands days after the State Department imposed sanctions on five Chinese companies connected to Linwei Ding, a former Google engineer convicted earlier this year of stealing trade secrets related to artificial intelligence. Beijing also objected to those penalties, saying they seriously harm the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese businesses. Taken together, the two moves underline Washington’s widening focus on technology and capital flows as a front in its rivalry with China. item.description:
The cut removes one of the most bullish institutional Kospi targets from the table, but the bank’s insistence on deep value gives contrarian investors a framework for buying into weakness rather than chasing the selloff lower. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix remain the swing factor, since any stabilisation in sentiment toward AI capital spending would likely feed directly into the index given their weight. The sector preferences point to a possible rotation inside Korean equities, away from memory chips and toward power, industrials and domestically focused names, which could limit the downside for the broader market even if chip stocks stay under pressure. Foreign investor flows will be the key signal of whether the valuation argument is gaining traction.

--- Goldman Sachs has blinked on its Kospi call but not folded, arguing that a market trading at about four times earnings is pricing in a chip downturn far worse than is likely.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs lowered its 12-month Kospi target to 9,000 from 12,000, a 25% cut, citing AI investment concerns and more conservative valuations
  • The index has fallen more than 35% from its June peak, and the new target still implies upside of more than 60%
  • The Kospi’s 12-month forward P/E has dropped to around four, a level not seen across 18 major markets since 2006, and roughly half the valuation of Indonesian stocks
  • Goldman estimates current chip valuations imply a 65% fall in sector earnings in 2027, which it considers overly pessimistic
  • Stocks outside memory chips, about half the index, trade at under eight times forward earnings
  • Preferred themes include power, industrials, corporate governance plays, domestic recovery and Korean popular culture

Goldman Sachs has cut its 12-month target for South Korea’s Kospi Index by a quarter, lowering it to 9,000 from 12,000, as worries over artificial intelligence spending and a shift toward more conservative equity valuations weigh on the market. Even so, the bank argues that Korean shares now look deeply undervalued, and its new target still implies a gain of more than 60% from current levels.

The downgrade follows a slide of more than 35% in the benchmark from its June peak. Goldman had raised its Kospi target in June and kept its bullish stance even as global technology stocks began to retreat on concerns about the scale of AI investment.

South Korea’s market has been especially exposed to that shift because of its heavy concentration in memory chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Both have been major beneficiaries of demand for chips used in AI infrastructure, which has turned the Kospi into a widely watched gauge of investor sentiment toward the technology. As concerns have grown about rising financing costs, enormous infrastructure outlays and uncertain returns on that spending, selling has spread across Korean equities.

Goldman’s strategists said the market is now discounting an excessively bleak outlook for corporate fundamentals. The Kospi’s 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to around four, a level not seen across 18 major markets since 2006, and Korean stocks now trade at roughly half the valuation of Indonesian equities. By the bank’s estimates, current semiconductor valuations imply a 65% collapse in sector earnings in 2027, a scenario the strategists regard as overly pessimistic.

The valuation argument extends beyond chips. Companies outside the memory sector, which make up about half the index, trade at under eight times forward earnings, according to the bank.

Despite trimming its headline target, Goldman continues to favour selected areas of the market, including power, industrials, stocks tied to corporate governance reform, and companies set to benefit from a domestic economic recovery and the global reach of Korean popular culture. Whether investors embrace that value case is likely to depend on how sentiment toward AI spending evolves in the months ahead. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Four hikes in, the RBA’s forecasting chief says the job is not finished, with war-driven oil costs working their way into supply chains and a fifth increase looking likely on November 3.

Summary:

  • She declined to pre-empt the board’s decision but said policymakers remain committed to getting inflation down; the next meeting is November 3

Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said the central bank has not yet finished its fight against inflation, reinforcing expectations that policymakers will raise interest rates again when they meet on November 3.

Speaking in an interview with Nine Network’s 60 Minutes, broadcast on Sunday evening Australian time, Hunter noted that the board had delivered four rate increases this year to tackle persistent price pressures. Asked whether that tightening had been enough to tame inflation, she replied “not quite yet.” She declined to front-run the board’s next decision, but stressed that policymakers remained committed to bringing inflation down.

Her remarks build on comments from Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser on Wednesday, when he said the inflation outlook had become materially worse since the bank’s August assessment. Those remarks had already lifted market expectations for a hike at the November meeting.

Hunter, who oversees economic forecasting at the RBA, pointed to the ongoing US-Iran war as a source of renewed pressure. Higher oil prices linked to the conflict are beginning to become embedded in some supply chains, she said, adding that the bank expects more of that pass-through to come. The comment suggests the RBA is increasingly concerned that the energy shock is spreading beyond fuel prices into the broader cost base of the economy, which would make inflation more persistent and harder to bring back down.

The RBA lifted its cash rate in late September to 4.6%, the highest level in 15 years. A further increase would add downward pressure on Australian property prices, which have already been falling. Hunter said the decline in house prices was not, so far, creating systemic financial stress across the system, a signal that the bank does not see housing weakness as a reason to hold off.

Attention now turns to Wednesday, when Australia’s third-quarter consumer price data are released. The trimmed mean measure of underlying inflation is expected at 3.6%, broadly in line with the previous quarter. Governor Michele Bullock and other policymakers are also scheduled to appear before parliament the same day, giving them another opportunity to set out their thinking ahead of the decision. A reading in line with forecasts, combined with the oil-driven pressure Hunter described, would likely leave a November hike as the market’s base case.

item.title: Trading on Margin: What It Means and How to Get Started
item.description:
Why trade Bitcoin if stocks can double? The leverage question traders miss

A trader recently asked: "Why trade Bitcoin? What's it gonna do, 2x, 3x? These days stocks can do that. So what's the point?"

It's a reasonable question, but it misses something fundamental about trading: leverage.

Traders don't necessarily need Bitcoin, gold or a stock to double in price to achieve a substantial percentage return on their trading capital. Depending on the financial instrument and the size of their position, even a relatively small price movement can have a significant impact on their account.

Unfortunately, that works in both directions. Leverage can accelerate profits, but it can also destroy a trading account surprisingly quickly.

Understanding how it works is one of the most important lessons in financial markets.

What is leverage in trading?

Leverage allows you to control a position worth more than the capital you commit to it.

Imagine you have $10,000 available for trading and expect Bitcoin to rise by 3%.

Without leverage (1x)

You purchase $10,000 worth of Bitcoin. If BTC rises 3%, your position gains $300, representing a 3% return on your capital.

If Bitcoin falls 3%, you lose $300 instead.

With 5x leverage

You use that same $10,000 as collateral to control a $50,000 Bitcoin position.

A 3% rise now generates a $1,500 profit, equivalent to 15% of your starting capital.

But a 3% decline produces a $1,500 loss, also 15% of your capital.

These are simplified examples before trading costs, financing and potential liquidation.

The important distinction is that Bitcoin didn't need to rise 15%. It only moved 3%, but leverage multiplied the impact on your capital.

And the same principle applies to stocks, gold, stock indices and other markets.

Stock trading: Your broker may offer 2x to 4x buying power

Many stock investors don't realize their brokerage account may provide additional buying power if they qualify for margin trading.

For U.S. margin accounts, the traditional Regulation T framework generally allows an investor to borrow up to 50% of the initial purchase price of eligible stocks.

That translates into approximately 2x buying power.

A trader with $10,000 in account equity could therefore purchase $20,000 of eligible shares, using $10,000 of their own equity and $10,000 borrowed from the broker.

A 10% rise in the position would generate approximately $2,000, or 20% of the original equity, before borrowing costs.

Conversely, a 10% decline would cost $2,000.

What about day traders?

Eligible stock day traders may have access to approximately 4x intraday buying power, depending on their broker, securities and margin requirements.

For example, Charles Schwab introduced an intraday buying-power framework in July 2026 under which eligible accounts can trade certain shares with a 25% maintenance margin requirement.

This can provide up to four times buying power during the session. However, positions that exceed overnight buying power must be reduced or closed before the broker's deadline.

There was also an important regulatory change in 2026. FINRA's new intraday margin standards became effective June 4, 2026, replacing the old pattern day trader framework, including its $25,000 minimum equity requirement. Brokers have until October 20, 2027, to complete the transition.

Some may therefore operate differently during this period. Higher, risk-based buying power may be available through portfolio margin for qualified accounts, but 4.5x is not a universal standard.

The practical lesson: Buying power is a ceiling, not a recommendation.

Having permission to purchase $40,000 of shares does not mean someone with $10,000 should automatically do so.

Futures trading: How micro S&P 500, Nasdaq and gold contracts use leverage

Futures introduce another form of leverage.

Unlike borrowing money to buy shares, futures traders deposit margin, which acts as collateral for a standardized contract. They don't need to pay the full notional value of the position upfront.

The Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) offers several smaller contracts known as micro futures.

Let's examine three examples. All index levels, gold prices and margin deposits below are hypothetical, rather than live market quotes or current broker margin requirements.

Micro E-mini S&P 500 futures (MES)

One MES contract represents $5 multiplied by the S&P 500 futures index level.

If that index is trading at 7,000, one contract gives approximately $35,000 in market exposure.

Every one-point move in the index produces a $5 profit or loss per contract.

Suppose the required initial margin is $3,000. That would represent about 11.7x exposure relative to the required deposit.

However, if your actual account contains $10,000, your effective leverage relative to total account equity is 3.5x.

Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures (MNQ)

One MNQ contract represents $2 multiplied by the Nasdaq-100 futures index level.

At a hypothetical index level of 25,000, one contract provides $50,000 of exposure.

Each index point is worth $2 per contract.

If the required initial margin were $5,000, the position would represent 10x the deposit.

A trader holding that single contract in an account with $10,000 equity would have 5x effective account leverage.

Micro Gold futures (MGC)

One Micro Gold contract represents 10 troy ounces of gold.

If gold trades at a hypothetical $4,000 per ounce, a contract represents $40,000 of exposure.

Every $1 movement in gold's price changes the contract's value by $10.

If initial margin were $2,000, that represents 20x exposure relative to the required deposit.

But with $10,000 of actual account equity, the position represents 4x effective account leverage.

Why futures margin can be misleading

Exchange margin requirements change with volatility and market conditions. Some futures brokers also offer much lower day-trading margins than the amounts required to hold positions overnight.

A broker might permit a substantial futures position with a relatively small intraday deposit. That does not reduce the dollar amount lost when the market moves against the position.

The contract determines the profit and loss per price movement, not the margin deposit.

Lower margin makes access easier. It does not make the market safer.

Micro contracts are useful because their smaller contract sizes help traders adjust exposure and manage exits. For further education, see our investingLive guide to using micro contracts for partial profits.

Gold and stock CFDs: How leverage works with XAUUSD

Another common trading product is the contract for difference, or CFD.

A CFD allows traders to speculate on changes in an underlying asset's price without owning that asset.

For example, a broker may offer XAUUSD, representing gold quoted in U.S. dollars, as a leveraged spot gold CFD.

The exact instrument and contract size depend on the provider, so the XAUUSD symbol alone does not establish the trading terms.

Under the standard European retail CFD restrictions, the applicable maximum leverage generally includes:

Gold: 20x

A $1,000 margin deposit can support approximately $20,000 in exposure. A 1% gold price movement changes the position's value by around $200, equivalent to 20% of the deposit.

Individual stock CFDs: 5x

A $1,000 deposit can support a $5,000 position in an eligible stock CFD. A 5% adverse movement would cost approximately $250, or 25% of the deposit.

Major equity indices: 20x

Major stock indices such as the S&P 500 generally qualify for leverage up to 20x under these retail CFD rules.

Major currency pairs: 30x

For certain major foreign exchange pairs, retail leverage can reach 30x.

These are regulatory limits, not guaranteed offerings. Brokers may impose stricter requirements. Other jurisdictions and professional-client classifications can have significantly different limits.

CFDs also involve costs such as spreads, potential commissions and overnight financing. European and UK retail regimes include protections such as margin close-out and negative balance protection.

Those protections matter, but they do not prevent a trader from losing the capital committed to trading. And watch one of the biggest risks for traders: overleverage.

Bitcoin and Ethereum: Is there leverage on Binance, Coinbase or Kraken?

Here we reach an important distinction.

Buying Bitcoin or Ethereum on a normal spot exchange does not automatically involve leverage.

If you purchase $5,000 of BTC/USD or ETH/USD using $5,000 of your own funds, you normally have a 1x position.

The exchange may also offer margin products, allowing eligible customers to borrow against collateral, or derivatives such as perpetual futures.

These are different trading products, even when they reference the same cryptocurrency.

Binance

On the global Binance platform, ordinary spot purchases are generally unleveraged.

Eligible users can separately access margin trading. Binance's isolated-margin system supports different leverage tiers, including up to 10x for certain eligible pairs and position sizes.

The service requires borrowing assets and involves interest charges and liquidation risk.

Leveraged futures are a separate product again. Binance.com and Binance.US do not offer identical services.

Coinbase

Ordinary Coinbase and Coinbase Advanced spot purchases are also generally 1x.

Coinbase additionally documents a separate spot-margin service offering up to 10x on eligible markets.

However, access is restricted. For U.S. customers, Coinbase states that spot margin generally requires Eligible Contract Participant status, which for individuals ordinarily means at least $10 million in qualifying investable assets.

Coinbase also offers leveraged perpetual futures in certain eligible non-U.S. jurisdictions, with different rules from spot trading.

Kraken

Kraken's ordinary spot trading is unleveraged unless the user accesses its separate margin service.

A notable development in 2026 was Kraken's introduction of spot-margin trading for eligible U.S. retail customers.

According to Kraken's published terms, selected U.S. retail markets include up to 20x on BTC/USD and 10x on ETH/USD.

Kraken also lists leveraged spot-margin pairs for eligible international customers, with the permitted multiplier varying by pair and jurisdiction.

In every case, traders need to distinguish spot purchases from leveraged spot-margin trades and perpetual derivatives.

With a 20x position, even a relatively small adverse price movement may trigger liquidation. Traders should not assume that a 5% move against them will simply produce a manageable loss on their deposited funds.

There may also be borrowing costs, forced liquidation and, depending on the product, losses exceeding the initial collateral.

Regulations differ substantially between countries. For example, the UK prohibits sales of crypto derivatives to retail customers, while European CFD-style limits may apply to certain crypto perpetual products.

Prop trading: Does a $50,000 funded account really mean $50,000?

Prop trading adds another dimension to buying power.

Traditional proprietary trading firms use their own capital to trade markets, typically with professional risk oversight.

Online funded-trader programs frequently operate differently. Many begin with paid evaluations in simulated trading environments, and some subsequent funded stages remain simulated even when participants can qualify for real monetary payouts.

Consider a $50,000 futures trading evaluation.

That figure may sound like a trader has $50,000 available to lose.

But that is often far from the truth.

For example, Topstep's published $50,000 Trading Combine has a $2,000 maximum loss limit.

The program's account-size label is not equivalent to unrestricted cash capital.

If a trader loses $500, they have already consumed 25% of that initial $2,000 loss allowance, despite a displayed $50,000 account size.

And if the permitted loss threshold trails upward after profitable sessions, the available risk cushion can become even more restrictive.

Some programs limit position sizes, impose additional daily loss limits, restrict activity around economic announcements or set payout conditions.

So when evaluating a prop firm, understanding the actual drawdown allowance is more important than being impressed by the advertised account size.

Why trade Bitcoin rather than a stock that might double?

Now let's return to the original question.

There is no guarantee that Bitcoin will double or triple, and a strong-performing stock may indeed deliver a much larger percentage gain over a particular period.

But the potential return of an asset and the return on a trader's capital are not necessarily the same thing.

Bitcoin may appeal to traders because of its liquidity, volatility, around-the-clock spot market access and price behavior. Equity indices, gold futures and individual stocks offer other characteristics and opportunities.

A trader may seek relatively small price movements, rather than waiting years for an asset to appreciate dramatically.

Leverage makes capital-efficient exposure possible, but it does not give Bitcoin an automatic advantage over stocks, or vice versa.

Nor does it make any trading strategy profitable.

The decision to trade Bitcoin should depend on the opportunity, liquidity, costs, expected volatility and risk management, rather than simply asking which asset is more likely to produce a 2x return.

The most important difference: How much can you actually afford to lose?

Consider a practical example involving Micro Nasdaq futures.

Suppose a trader plans to buy one MNQ contract and place a stop 50 index points below the entry.

Since one contract is worth $2 per index point, the planned loss is:

50 points × $2 = $100 per contract.

With three contracts, the planned loss rises to $300.

On a $10,000 account, that is 3% of the account, before fees and any slippage.

The broker may permit more contracts, but the trader should decide how much risk is acceptable before determining position size.

A stop-loss is not a guarantee of execution at the selected price. Fast price movements, gaps and thin liquidity can create larger losses.

This leads to a useful distinction:

Available leverage: How much exposure your broker or exchange permits.

Effective leverage: How much exposure you actually hold compared with your account equity.

Trade risk: How much money you stand to lose if the trading idea fails and the position is exited, including the possibility of a worse-than-planned execution.

These are three different numbers. Successful risk management depends on understanding all three.

Is trading without leverage really trading?

Yes. Buying and selling fully paid shares or cryptocurrency is still trading, and professionals also use unleveraged positions when appropriate.

Leverage is not a requirement for being a professional trader.

However, leverage is a central feature of many active trading strategies, particularly in futures, foreign exchange, derivatives and capital-efficient portfolio management.

It allows traders to gain exposure to meaningful market movements without committing the full notional value of each position.

That flexibility helps explain its widespread use, but it also introduces a major source of risk.

The real skill is not obtaining the highest leverage. It is knowing how much exposure is appropriate for the trade, the account and the potential loss.

A trader does not need Bitcoin to triple, or a stock to double, to find a worthwhile trading opportunity.

But they do need to understand what happens to their capital when the market moves against them.

And sometimes, the most professional decision is not to use the leverage available at all.

Educational content only. Trading and investing involve risk of loss. Leveraged positions can result in rapid liquidation and, depending on the product, losses greater than the initial amount deposited.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Record ETF Inflows, Yet Stock Market Leadership Is Shifting. What's Going On?
item.description:
Stock market sector rotation: Energy leads while communication services suffers a sharp decline

U.S. stock market leadership is becoming increasingly selective. Three trading sessions reveal important differences between sectors, and even between industries within the same sector.

U.S. stocks are showing a notable change in leadership. Between the October 20 and October 23, 2026 closes, the Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE) gained 2.00%, while the Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLC) fell 4.25%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) declined 1.18% over the same period.

For stock investors and traders, the message is not simply that the market is falling. Some sectors are attracting buying interest while others are struggling, and these differences may help identify where the next opportunities and risks develop.

What the latest sector performance tells us

Energy was the strongest of the 11 major U.S. stock market sectors over the three sessions, followed by utilities, which gained 1.62%.

Consumer staples, real estate, financials and materials also finished higher. Together, these six sectors outperformed a declining S&P 500 benchmark.

The weakest performances came from communication services, consumer discretionary stocks, industrials and technology.

The particularly interesting development is the gap between the leaders and laggards. Energy outperformed communication services by 6.25 percentage points in just three sessions.

That is a substantial short-term divergence, although three trading days alone are insufficient to establish a durable rotation.

Why communication services is worth watching

Communication services was not merely the worst-performing sector over this period. Its sector ETF, XLC, declined in all three sessions:

  • Wednesday, October 21: -1.11%

  • Thursday, October 22: -1.42%

  • Friday, October 23: -1.78%

The selling was persistent, with the daily declines becoming larger.

One important contributor was Meta Platforms. After the company disclosed plans for additional financing alongside substantial AI investment commitments, investors became increasingly concerned about how much capital the next phase of AI development would require.

Reuters reported substantial selling in Meta and several other AI-related companies as investors reconsidered financing costs and the potential returns from enormous infrastructure investments.

There was also pressure on telecommunications companies amid reporting about potential new competition in wireless services.

However, communication services includes very different businesses, from digital advertising platforms to traditional telecom providers and entertainment companies. Weak sector performance does not mean every constituent faces the same problem.

What to watch:Whether XLC continues underperforming SPY after the initial selling pressure fades. A sustained recovery in relative performance would weaken the current bearish interpretation. Continued underperformance, even on days when the broader market advances, would be more concerning.

Energy is leading, but is it too late to chase?

Energy's 2.00% three-session gain was supported by a particularly strong Friday, when XLE advanced 2.60%.

Oil prices rose sharply amid renewed concerns about disruptions to Middle Eastern supplies. Brent crude reached approximately $116.72 per barrel on October 23, according to Reuters reporting.

Higher oil prices can support the earnings outlook for some energy producers. But the relationship is not equally favorable for all energy companies, particularly those facing higher operating costs or differing refining economics.

There is another reason to be selective.

Although the broader energy ETF has shown strong performance, the supplied market research indicates that buying interest has not been equally distributed across energy-related investments. Some exploration-focused products experienced withdrawals even as XLE attracted fresh ETF creations.

That creates an important distinction between a strong sector and an attractive new entry price.

For traders, a pullback that holds support and attracts renewed buying may offer more useful confirmation than purchasing immediately after a sharp advance.

For longer-term investors, sustained commodity prices, company cash flows, valuations and balance-sheet quality matter more than a three-day ETF performance ranking.

The surprising split within technology: Semiconductors versus software

Technology offers perhaps the most useful lesson from this market rotation.

While the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK) declined 1.19% over the three sessions, its underlying industries performed very differently.

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) fell approximately 3.51%, while the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) gained approximately 3.42%.

That is a difference of nearly seven percentage points.

This matters because headlines about technology selling can obscure substantial changes in leadership within the sector.

Investors appear to be distinguishing more carefully between businesses exposed to expensive AI infrastructure investment and other technology companies with different revenue, margin and capital requirements.

It would be premature to interpret this as an abandonment of AI. Friday's stabilization in several semiconductor shares also suggests that buying interest has not disappeared entirely.

A more useful question is whether software continues outperforming semiconductors over subsequent sessions, or whether chip stocks regain their earlier leadership.

For stock selection, that distinction could prove more actionable than simply deciding whether technology is bullish or bearish.

Defensive sectors are holding up, but leadership is not necessarily stable

Utilities rose 1.62% across the three sessions, while consumer staples gained 0.58%.

Both sectors are often considered defensive because electricity, food and household products generally remain necessary even when the economy slows.

However, their performance was not consistently positive throughout the period.

Consumer staples rallied 3.31% on Thursday, then declined 1.92% on Friday. Utilities also retreated on Friday.

In addition, Treasury yields remained elevated, with the U.S. 10-year yield approaching 5%. Higher yields can compete with dividend-paying equities and make financing more expensive for rate-sensitive businesses, including utilities and real estate.

This creates a more nuanced picture than a straightforward flight into defensive stocks.

Relative strength is not the same as absolute strength.A sector can outperform a falling S&P 500 and still lose money, while a sector that recently outperformed may become vulnerable if investors have already crowded into the trade.

Three scenarios investors and traders can monitor next week

1. The rotation continues

Energy maintains relative strength, communication services continues to underperform, and leadership remains concentrated outside previous market favorites.

That would support continued attention to selective energy exposure and caution toward weaker communication-services stocks. The quality of the entry still matters, particularly following large short-term moves.

2. Technology leadership broadens again

Semiconductors recover, technology begins consistently outperforming SPY, and communication services stabilizes.

That would suggest the recent weakness may have been a temporary reassessment of valuations and investment spending rather than the beginning of a more lasting shift.

3. Weakness spreads to more sectors

Consumer discretionary and industrials remain under pressure, while the recent defensive winners also begin to weaken.

In that scenario, investors may become less concerned about which sector is leading and more concerned about whether overall equity market conditions are deteriorating. Market breadth, the number of stocks rising versus falling, would be particularly useful to follow.

The investor takeaway: Follow the rotation, but look beneath the surface

One of the most useful aspects of sector analysis is that it can reveal differences the headline S&P 500 performance does not show.

Over these three sessions, the benchmark declined 1.18%, but the experience of an energy investor was very different from that of an investor concentrated in communication services.

The same applies within technology, where software and semiconductors moved in opposite directions.

This does not automatically make the strongest sector a buy or the weakest sector a short. The stronger opportunity may be found by examining whether leadership is broadening, whether pullbacks attract buyers and whether weaker sectors can recover relative to the market.

The next several sessions, particularly alongside major technology earnings and the Federal Reserve's October 27-28 meeting, should provide further evidence about whether this is a temporary rotation or the beginning of a more sustained change in stock market leadership.

For now, the central question is worth keeping on the watchlist: Are investors simply rotating within the market, or is weakness in former leaders beginning to spread?

What I find interesting: Record ETF inflows, but investors are becoming more selective

What I find interesting about the latest sector rotation is how it contrasts with the bigger picture of money flowing into exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

According to ETFGI's finalized September 2026 figures, U.S.-listed ETFs attracted $152.93 billion during September, bringing year-to-date inflows to a record $1.56 trillion. Europe attracted another $51.04 billion during September, taking its year-to-date total to a record $432.45 billion.

Both regions had already exceeded their previous full-year inflow records with three months of 2026 remaining.

Yet something else happened: total ETF assets declined slightly in both regions during September, despite all that new money coming in.

U.S. ETF assets decreased from $16.36 trillion at the end of August to $16.24 trillion in September. European ETF assets slipped from $3.97 trillion to $3.94 trillion.

That illustrates an important distinction for investors. Money can continue flowing into investment products while the market value of their holdings falls. New investments and investment returns are two different things.

Where is the money going?

The composition of September's inflows also provides an interesting clue about changing investor preferences.

In the United States:

  • Equity ETFs: $41.02 billion in September inflows.

  • Fixed-income ETFs: $40.08 billion, almost matching equities.

  • Commodity ETFs: $3.74 billion.

  • Actively managed ETFs: $61.16 billion, representing a particularly strong area of demand.

Active ETFs are an investment-management category that can include equities and bonds, so these figures should not be added together.

Europe showed a similar appetite for diversification, attracting $26.30 billion into equity ETFs and $9.41 billion into fixed income.

Another notable development is that both regions attracted fewer total ETF inflows in September than in August, despite their record-breaking annual performance.

Does that mean investors are becoming more cautious? Possibly, but flows alone cannot establish their intentions.

The nearly equal U.S. equity and fixed-income inflows are nevertheless worth watching. Investors can continue participating in stocks while simultaneously increasing exposure to bonds, potentially balancing growth opportunities with income and diversification.

What does this tell us about the latest stock sector rotation?

The October sector-performance figures show energy substantially outperforming communication services, while technology itself is dividing between stronger software stocks and weaker semiconductors.

The September ETF data offers a broader perspective: strong overall investment demand does not mean that every sector, asset class or individual stock will attract equal interest.

Even within September's ETF flows, concentration was striking. Just 20 U.S. ETFs attracted a combined $81.34 billion, with SPY alone accounting for $10.70 billion.

And in Europe, an inverse leveraged oil product attracted $6.10 billion. This product is designed to benefit from falling oil futures prices, illustrating how some ETF-related investments express tactical bearish positions rather than conventional long-term ownership.

Importantly, September's regional flows cannot explain or confirm the specific sector movements of October 21-23. They cover different periods and different groups of investments. But they do provide context for why examining where money is flowing can be as useful as examining how much is flowing.

A lesson worth remembering

ETF flows tell us where net new money is entering or leaving investment products. They do not prove why investors acted, guarantee future returns or necessarily identify which stocks will outperform next.

For traders, watching sector performance alongside more recent, sector-specific ETF flows could help determine whether a developing rotation is gaining support or losing momentum.

For longer-term investors, the record-breaking annual inflows suggest continued demand for ETFs as investment vehicles. But the performance, valuation and risk of the assets inside those funds remain crucial.

What I find most interesting is that money can be pouring into ETFs at record levels while leadership underneath the stock market is changing dramatically. The opportunity is not necessarily to follow the biggest inflow or buy yesterday's strongest sector, but to recognize where durable leadership may be developing, and where it may be fading.
